title: Do the misses add up to much?
hook: A few hits sell the most. Can 99,000 slow sellers still matter?

knows: a few hits sell a lot
doesNotKnow: that under a Zipf law the 99% of items outside the top 1% can still take over a third of all sales

misconception: Outside the hits, sales are negligible.
objective: The learner can explain that with sales ∝ 1/rank over 100,000 items the top 1,000 take 61.9% and the other 99,000 take 38.1%, because every tenfold range of ranks sells about the same total.

claims.text: With sales proportional to 1/rank over 100,000 items, the top 1,000 take 61.9% of sales and the other 99,000 take 38.1%.
claims.source: Demo.tsx share(): harmonic sums H(1,000)/H(100,000) = 7.4855/12.0901 = 0.6191. Builder's Node run 2026-10-14; matches the brief (0.619). The stage also shows top 1 8.3%, top 10 24.2%, top 100 42.9%, top 10,000 81.0%. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): Own node harmonic sums: H(1000) = 7.4855, H(100000) = 12.0901, share 61.91% / 38.09%. Top 1 8.27%, 10 24.23%, 100 42.91%, 10,000 80.96%. Matches Demo share().

claims.text: Each of the items outside the top 1,000 sells under 1/1,000 as much as the best seller.
claims.source: Item of rank r sells 1/r of item 1; r ≥ 1,001 gives at most 1/1,001. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): Rank r >= 1,001 sells 1/r <= 1/1,001 < 1/1,000 of item 1.

claims.text: Items 1,001–10,000 sell about as much in total as items 11–100 (19.0% vs 18.7%), and so do items 10,001–100,000; each tenfold stretch of ranks adds about the same.
claims.source: Harmonic sums (builder's Node run, 2026-10-14): ranks 1–10 24.2%, 11–100 18.7%, 101–1,000 19.0%, 1,001–10,000 19.0%, 10,001–100,000 19.0%. Each tenfold range sums to about ln 10 = 2.30 out of 12.09. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): Own node sums: 11-100 18.68%, 101-1,000 19.01%, 1,001-10,000 19.04%, 10,001-100,000 19.04% (raw 2.258, 2.298, 2.302, 2.303 vs ln 10 = 2.3026). Ranks 1-10 are 24.2%, so 'each tenfold stretch about the same' holds from 11 on; the sentence's comparisons are all from 11 on.

claims.text: A store that can stock them all gains over a third of its sales from items a small shelf would drop.
claims.source: Within the lesson's model: a shelf holding only the top 1,000 forgoes 38.1% of sales (c1). Model consequence, not a measured store. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): Follows from c1 inside the model: dropping ranks 1,001+ loses 38.1% > 1/3.

claims.text: The name "long tail" was popularised by Chris Anderson.
claims.source: C. Anderson, 'The Long Tail', Wired 12.10 (2004), and the book The Long Tail (2006); Easley and Kleinberg (2010) ch. 18. From the brief; builder has not opened these. Attribution: fact-checker confirms. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): Web search 2026-10-14 (Wikipedia 'The Long Tail (book)', Reason 2006, historyofinformation.com): Anderson's article 'The Long Tail', Wired 12.10, October 2004, expanded into the 2006 book. Original Wired page not opened. E&K (2010) ch. 18 (Power Laws and Rich-Get-Richer Phenomena) has a Long Tail section: placement from memory, host blocked, confident.

claims.text: The 1/rank curve is a model, not any store's data.
claims.source: Lesson rule: sales(r) ∝ 1/r is assumed, not fitted. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): Demo.tsx uses 1/r for all 100,000 ranks with no data; reveal states it is a model.

recall.question: Sales fall as 1/rank across 100,000 items. Roughly what share of all sales do the 99,000 items outside the top 1,000 take?
recall.why: Each tenfold range of ranks sells about the same total (about 19%), and the two ranges beyond rank 1,000 add up to about 38%.
